framework.name: Senior Dog Longevity Monitoring Framework
framework.premise: Most decline in aging dogs is caught late because nobody was measuring. A twice-yearly structured review across a fixed set of domains catches trends while they are still reversible, and turns a vague 'she's slowing down' into a dated number a veterinarian can act on.
framework.cadence_default: Every 6 months from age 7 (or from age 5 for giant breeds), and every 3 months from age 11 or after any new diagnosis.
framework.how_to_use: Score every domain at each review, even the ones that seem fine — the value is in the trend, not the snapshot. A domain that moves two levels between reviews matters more than a domain that has been mildly abnormal for years.

domains.name: Body weight, body condition, and muscle mass
domains.why: Excess weight measurably worsens arthritis pain, and losing 6-9% of body weight reduces lameness on its own. Muscle loss is a separate problem that tracks with frailty and is routinely missed because a fat dog and a sarcopenic dog can weigh the same.
domains.measure: Body weight in kg on the same scale; Body Condition Score (1-9); Muscle Condition Score (normal / mild / moderate / severe loss) assessed over the skull, scapulae, spine, and pelvis.
domains.instrument: WSAVA Body Condition Score and Muscle Condition Score charts
domains.cadence: Monthly weight at home; BCS and MCS at every review
domains.target: BCS 4-5 of 9, with normal muscle condition
red_flags: Unexplained weight loss of more than 5% between reviews
Muscle loss progressing while body weight stays flat
Weight gain despite unchanged feeding

domains.name: Mobility and chronic pain
domains.why: Osteoarthritis is the most common source of chronic pain in older dogs and the best-studied condition in canine geriatric medicine. Owners consistently under-report it because they read it as ordinary aging rather than pain.
domains.measure: A validated owner questionnaire scored the same way each time, plus three concrete observations: time to rise from lying, willingness to use stairs, and longest comfortable walk.
domains.instrument: Canine Brief Pain Inventory (CBPI), LOAD, or Canine Orthopaedic Index — pick one and stay with it
domains.cadence: Every review; every 4 weeks when starting or changing a pain medication
domains.target: Stable or improving score; any pain treatment should produce a measurable change or be reconsidered
red_flags: Reluctance to rise, or taking more than a few seconds to stand
New avoidance of stairs, jumping, or slippery floors
Night restlessness or panting at rest, both of which can be pain rather than anxiety
Sudden worsening in a dog on an anti-NGF antibody, which cannot be withdrawn quickly

domains.name: Cognition and behavior
domains.why: Cognitive dysfunction is under-diagnosed because early signs read as ordinary aging. It is also the domain where a baseline score matters most, since gradual change is invisible without one.
domains.measure: A validated cognitive questionnaire covering disorientation, social interaction, sleep-wake cycle, house-training, activity, and anxiety.
domains.cadence: Every review; at 30 and 90 days after starting a dietary or drug intervention
domains.target: Stable score. The 2018 MCT diet trial measured change at 30 and 90 days, so judge interventions on that timescale rather than in weeks.
red_flags: Staring at walls, getting stuck in corners, or standing on the hinge side of doors
Reversed day-night sleep pattern
House-soiling in a previously reliable dog
Failing to greet familiar people

domains.name: Thirst, urination, and appetite
domains.why: Increased drinking and urination is the earliest owner-detectable sign of kidney disease, diabetes, and Cushing's — three conditions where early detection changes the outcome substantially.
domains.measure: Measured water intake in ml over 24 hours (not estimated), overnight accidents, and appetite change.
domains.instrument: Household measuring jug; normal intake is roughly under 100 ml/kg/day and most healthy dogs drink well below that
domains.cadence: A measured 24-hour water intake before each review, and any time you suspect a change
domains.target: Stable intake appropriate to diet and weather
red_flags: Water intake above 100 ml/kg/day
New overnight urination in a house-trained dog
Appetite increase with weight loss, or appetite loss of more than a couple of days

domains.name: Bloodwork, urinalysis, and organ function
domains.why: Every drug on this site that works long-term is limited by organ tolerance rather than by efficacy. NSAID use in particular requires a baseline and repeat monitoring, and kidney disease is usually well advanced before it is visible from the outside.
domains.measure: Complete blood count, serum chemistry, urinalysis with urine specific gravity, and SDMA. Thyroid testing where signs suggest it.
domains.instrument: Veterinary laboratory panel — keep copies of every result so trends are visible across years
domains.cadence: Annually as a baseline from age 7; every 6 months from age 11; within 2-4 weeks of starting an NSAID and every 3-6 months while on one
domains.target: Values stable within reference range; a value drifting within the normal range still matters
red_flags: Rising creatinine or SDMA, even inside the reference interval
Urine specific gravity falling toward 1.012
New or rising liver enzymes in a dog on long-term medication

domains.name: Heart and breathing
domains.why: Resting respiratory rate is the single most useful number an owner can collect at home, and a rise above 30 breaths per minute while sleeping is an early, actionable sign of congestive heart failure.
domains.measure: Sleeping respiratory rate — count chest rises for 30 seconds while the dog is asleep and double it. Note any cough, exercise intolerance, or fainting.
domains.instrument: A phone timer, recorded weekly in a log
domains.cadence: Weekly at home for any dog with a known murmur; monthly otherwise
domains.target: Under 30 breaths per minute while sleeping
red_flags: Sleeping respiratory rate consistently above 30
Any collapse or fainting episode — same-day veterinary attention
Cough that worsens at night, or reduced exercise tolerance

domains.name: Dental and oral health
domains.why: Periodontal disease is painful, extremely common in older dogs, and frequently rationalized as 'old dog breath'. It is also one of the few sources of chronic pain that can be genuinely resolved rather than managed.
domains.measure: Visual check of gums and teeth for tartar, recession, mobility, and masses; note breath odor, dropped food, and one-sided chewing.
domains.instrument: Veterinary oral exam; conscious inspection at home between visits
domains.cadence: Every review, with professional assessment annually
red_flags: Dropping food, chewing on one side, or reluctance to take hard treats
Any oral mass
Facial swelling below the eye, which suggests a tooth root abscess

domains.name: Lumps, masses, and skin
domains.why: Cancer risk climbs steeply with age. A dated body map turns 'has this always been there?' into an answerable question, which is the difference between early and late detection.
domains.measure: A full-body check with each mass logged by location and measured in mm, ideally photographed against a ruler.
domains.instrument: Body map diagram with dated measurements
domains.cadence: Monthly at home; every review with a veterinarian
red_flags: Any new mass, or an existing one that changes size, shape, or texture
Masses that are fixed to underlying tissue, ulcerated, or growing quickly
Any mass in a dog that is also losing weight

domains.name: Vision and hearing
domains.why: Sensory loss mimics cognitive dysfunction almost exactly — a dog that ignores you may be deaf rather than demented, and the management is completely different. This must be excluded before a dementia diagnosis is accepted.
domains.measure: Response to hand signals versus voice, navigation in dim light, startle response when approached from behind, bumping into furniture in unfamiliar places.
domains.instrument: Structured observation; veterinary ophthalmic exam where change is suspected
red_flags: Bumping into things, especially in low light
Cloudiness of the lens, or a visibly enlarged or reddened eye — the latter is urgent
Not responding to a name that used to work reliably

domains.name: Medication and supplement review
domains.why: Geriatric dogs accumulate medications, and the interaction risks are real — selegiline with serotonergic drugs, NSAIDs with steroids or with a second NSAID. Reviews are also the moment to drop supplements that trials show do not work.
domains.measure: A complete list of everything given, including supplements, chews, and over-the-counter products, with dose and reason.
domains.instrument: Written medication list brought to every visit
domains.cadence: Every review, and any time something is added
red_flags: Two NSAIDs, or an NSAID plus a corticosteroid
An MAO inhibitor such as selegiline alongside tramadol or a serotonergic antidepressant
Any supplement continued for over a year with no measured benefit

domains.name: Quality of life
domains.why: The hardest decisions get made in crisis, at night, without a reference point. Scoring quality of life while the dog is doing well creates a baseline and forces the conversation to happen before it is urgent.
domains.measure: Score hurt, hunger, hydration, hygiene, happiness, mobility, and whether good days outnumber bad — each 0 to 10.
domains.cadence: Every review; weekly in advanced disease or on hospice care
domains.target: A total consistently above 35 of 70 is generally considered acceptable quality of life, but the trend and the owner's own read matter more than the threshold
red_flags: Bad days beginning to outnumber good days
Any single category persistently at or below 3
Loss of interest in the two or three things the dog has always loved most

domains.name: Activity and sleep
domains.why: Activity decline is often the first objective signal of pain or systemic illness, and it can be measured continuously rather than recalled. Sleep disruption cuts across pain, cognition, and cardiac disease.
domains.measure: Daily activity from a collar accelerometer if available, otherwise total walk minutes per week; night waking episodes per week.
domains.instrument: Activity monitor or a simple weekly log
domains.cadence: Continuous where a device is used; otherwise a one-week log before each review
red_flags: A sustained drop in activity not explained by weather or routine
Increased night waking or pacing
Sleeping through activities that used to prompt engagement
